result.markdown: --- title: "Does a protective skin microbiome save the population?" subtitle: "Building the model one piece of biology at a time" engine: julia --- ## The question Amphibians can be treated with skin bacteria that inhibit the chytrid fungi *Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis* (Bd) and *B. salamandrivorans* (Bsal). Would that protect a population? This vignette answers the question several times over. It starts from the simplest possible description of treatment and adds one piece of biology at each step. After every step it asks the same question again, so that the effect of each added piece of realism can be seen. Two systems are followed in parallel: - **Bsal in fire salamanders**, starting from the model of Schmidt et al. (2017); - **Bd in common toads**, starting from the model of Mitchell et al. (2008). ::: {.callout-important} The two starting models are published and are reproduced here from their papers. Everything added to them is new work in this package and **is not a published result**. Values taken from experiments are read from the package's parameter compendium and are named where they are used. All other added values (efficacy, coverage, spread, exposure windows) are illustrative: they show what the model does, not what a real treatment would achieve. ::: ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Chytridiomycosis, Plots, Printf default(linewidth = 2, size = (720, 380), legendfontsize = 8, guidefontsize = 9, titlefontsize = 10, left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 4Plots.mm) T(; kw...) = MicrobiomeTreatment(; kw...) # One row per step, filled in as we go and shown as a table at the end. ladder = NamedTuple[] step!(system, n, added, outcome, note) = push!(ladder, (; system, n, added, outcome, note)) function ladder_plot(system, xlabel) rows = filter(r -> r.system == system, ladder) labels = ["$(r.n). $(r.added)" for r in rows] bar([r.outcome for r in rows]; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:length(rows), labels), yflip = true, legend = false, xlabel, xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, size = (820, 70 + 34 * length(rows)), left_margin = 6Plots.mm, color = :steelblue) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ladder_plot (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ## Part A. Bsal in fire salamanders The outcome throughout Part A is the **mean number of adults over the ten years after Bsal arrives, as a fraction of carrying capacity**. A value of 1 means the population was untouched. ### Step 0. The host and the pathogen Schmidt et al. (2017) describe adult female salamanders as susceptible, latent or infectious. Infectious animals die within about a week. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p = SchmidtParameters(:schmidt2017) @printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p)) sli(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticSLIProblem(p, tr; kw...)) a0 = sli(T()) step!("Bsal", 0, "no treatment", a0.mean_hosts, "population collapses within a year") plot(a0.t, a0.hosts ./ p.K; xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", label = "no treatment", xlims = (0, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R0 = 24.8 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: With a reproduction number near 25 the population collapses. ### Step 1. A treated class The simplest description of treatment: an animal is either treated or not, and a treated animal is infected less often. Every adult is treated once, on the day Bsal arrives, with a treatment that blocks 99% of infections and lasts for life. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} block = T(efficacy = 0.99) @printf("coverage needed to stop Bsal invading: %.2f\n", critical_coverage(p, block)) a1 = sli(block; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 1, "treated class: blocks 99% of infection, for life", a1.mean_hosts, "treated adults are safe; their offspring are not") plot(a1.t, [a1.hosts a1.treated] ./ p.K; label = ["all adults" "treated adults"], xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "fraction of K") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` coverage needed to stop Bsal invading: 0.97 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The treated adults survive, but the population still declines. Recruits are born untreated and Bsal is still circulating, so each generation of treated animals is replaced by unprotected ones. ### Step 2. Protection is lost Applied bacteria do not stay for life. Here a treated animal reverts to untreated with a half-life of one year. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} a2 = sli(T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0); coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 2, "+ protection lost, half-life 1 year", a2.mean_hosts, "collapse is only delayed") a2.mean_hosts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.13396963041084453 ``` ::: ::: ### Step 3. The microbiome spreads between animals If treated animals pass the bacteria to others, protection can reach the recruits. The microbiome then has its own reproduction number: the number of animals one treated animal passes it to before losing it. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} spread = T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0) @printf("microbiome reproduction number %.0f, long-run coverage %.2f\n", microbiome_reproduction_number(spread; turnover = p.b), equilibrium_coverage(spread; turnover = p.b)) a3 = sli(spread; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 3, "+ microbiome spreads between animals", a3.mean_hosts, "full protection: the microbiome maintains itself") plot(a0.t, a0.hosts ./ p.K; label = "0. no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", legend = :right) plot!(a1.t, a1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "1. treated class, for life") plot!(a2.t, a2.hosts ./ p.K; label = "2. + lost with half-life 1 yr") plot!(a3.t, a3.hosts ./ p.K; label = "3. + spreads between animals") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` microbiome reproduction number 46, long-run coverage 0.98 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: At this level of realism the conclusion would be: **a self-spreading, strongly protective microbiome works, and nothing else does.** ### Step 4. What trials actually show: survival, not fewer infections In challenge trials, treated animals were infected as often as untreated ones, but fewer died. In one trial of *Rana muscosa*, the compendium records these counts: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} h = parameter_set(:harris2009ismej) mortality_reduction(h.deaths_treated, h.n_treated, h.deaths_control, h.n_control) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (median = 0.9525115575081867, lower = 0.554197905634275, upper = 0.9998880034962464) ``` ::: ::: So the treated class is changed: instead of blocking infection, treatment reduces disease-induced death (`tolerance`). A treated, infected animal stays infectious. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} tolerant = T(tolerance = 0.9, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0) @printf("Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: %.0f (untreated %.0f)\n", effective_reproduction_number(p, tolerant, 1.0), basic_reproduction_number(p)) a4 = sli(tolerant; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 4, "+ protection as in trials: survive, still infected", a4.mean_hosts, "fails, and raises transmission: survivors shed for longer") a4.mean_hosts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: 232 (untreated 25) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.020566192434802892 ``` ::: ::: The same spreading microbiome now fails. Animals that survive infection shed for longer, so Bsal's reproduction number goes up, not down. ### Step 5. Lower pathogen load: less death and less shedding A microbiome that suppresses the fungus should lower the load on the animal. Lower load means less shedding as well as less death. Here both follow from one reduction in load: shedding in proportion to load, death in proportion to load raised to a power `k`. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} reductions = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999] ks = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0] R = [effective_reproduction_number(p, load_reducing_treatment(ρ; death_exponent = k), 1.0) for ρ in reductions, k in ks] plot(string.(reductions), R; yscale = :log10, marker = :circle, xlabel = "reduction in load", ylabel = "Bsal reproduction number, all treated", label = permutedims(["k = $k" for k in ks]), legend = :topright) hline!([1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "threshold") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: With death proportional to load (`k = 1`) the two effects nearly cancel: the animal sheds less but for longer. Only a very large reduction brings the reproduction number below 1. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} a5 = sli(load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0); coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 5, "+ lower load (99%): less death and less shedding", a5.mean_hosts, "partial; survivors remain infected") (mean_adults = a5.mean_hosts, final_prevalence = a5.final_prevalence) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (mean_adults = 0.17958281415555719, final_prevalence = 0.1329268012959979) ``` ::: ::: ### Step 6. Larvae Schmidt's model has adults only. Fire salamander larvae can be infected experimentally without showing disease, and half of them carried the infection through metamorphosis (Wang et al. 2021; the count is read from the compendium). ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} stage = BsalLarvalStage(:wang2021; adult_to_larva = 5.2) @printf("carry-over through metamorphosis: %.1f\n", stage.carry_over) b0 = solve(BsalLarvalProblem(p, stage)) plot(a0.t, max.(a0.hosts ./ p.K, 1e-12); yscale = :log10, label = "adults only (step 0)", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", legend = :bottomright) plot!(b0.t, b0.adults ./ p.K; label = "with a larval stage") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` carry-over through metamorphosis: 0.5 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Adding the stage changes the untreated outcome. Larvae already in the water metamorphose after the adult epidemic has burnt out, so the population no longer falls to vanishingly small numbers. The near-extinction in the adults-only model was partly a result of having no other stage. Treatment is now put on this model, going back to the infection-blocking treatment of step 1 so that the effect of the stage itself is clear. ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} lar(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticLarvalProblem(p, stage, tr; coverage = 1.0, kw...)) a6 = lar(block) step!("Bsal", 6, "+ larval stage (treatment as in step 1)", a6.mean_adults, "as step 1: recruits still unprotected") a6.mean_adults ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.33434708829646337 ``` ::: ::: ### Step 7. Treat the right stage With larvae in the model, treatment can be given to them too. Two new unknowns link the stages: whether a treated larva keeps the bacteria through metamorphosis (`retention`), and whether a treated mother's larvae are born with them (`maternal`). ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} quarterly = 0:0.25:9.75 strategies = [ ("adults, once", (;)), ("larvae, quarterly; lost at metamorphosis", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly)), ("larvae, quarterly; kept", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)), ("both stages, quarterly; kept", (treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)), ] vals = [lar(block; kw...).mean_adults for (_, kw) in strategies] bar(vals; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(strategies)), yflip = true, legend = false, xlabel = "mean adults (fraction of K)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} a7 = lar(block; treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 7, "+ treat both stages, kept through metamorphosis", a7.mean_adults, "full protection with no spread at all") a7.mean_adults ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.9999385316733599 ``` ::: ::: This overturns the conclusion of step 3. Once recruits can be treated before they become adults, **the microbiome does not need to spread**. It does need to survive metamorphosis, and that has not been measured. ### Step 8. How long the bacteria really last Two open datasets (a field trial in *Rana sierrae* and a laboratory trial in *Xenopus laevis*) give the abundance of applied bacteria over time. Fitting an exponential decline to them gives half-lives of 3 to 14 days; in the field, 4 to 5 days. (The fits are this project's own and are described in the project wiki.) Protection now wanes with abundance. `protective_fold` is how far abundance can fall before half the effect is lost; nobody has measured it, so three values are shown. ::: {#28 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} days = 0:1:150 plot(xlabel = "days since application", ylabel = "fraction of full protection", legend = :topright) for F in (10.0, 100.0, 1000.0) w = T(efficacy = 0.99, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = F) plot!(days, [protection(w, d / 365) for d in days]; label = @sprintf("fold %g: half gone after %.0f days", F, 365 * protection_duration(w))) end current() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} waning = T(efficacy = 0.99, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0) a8 = lar(waning; treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0) step!("Bsal", 8, "+ measured decay (half-life 5 days), dosed quarterly", a8.mean_adults, "fails: protection lasts about a month; monthly dosing reaches 0.28") monthly = lar(waning; treat = :both, treat_times = 0:(1 / 12):9.95, retention = 1.0) (quarterly = a8.mean_adults, monthly = monthly.mean_adults) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (quarterly = 0.06364264021907155, monthly = 0.2817745379332257) ``` ::: ::: ### Part A summary ::: {#32 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ladder_plot("Bsal", "mean adults over 10 years, fraction of K") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Part B. Bd in common toads The outcome throughout Part B is the **number of adults over the last ten of 35 years, as a fraction of the number without Bd**, together with whether Bd persists. The parameter set is the one behind Figure 2d of Mitchell et al. (2008), in which Bd drives the toads extinct and then dies out itself. ### Step 0. The host and the pathogen In Mitchell's model only tadpoles are infected. Infected tadpoles are removed at metamorphosis, and zoospores live in the pond. ::: {#34 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} m = MitchellParameters(:mitchell2008; set = "fig2d") pond(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticPondProblem(m, tr; kw...)) rel(r) = r.A_mean / r.A_disease_free show_pond(r) = (adults = round(rel(r), digits = 2), toads_persist = r.toads_persist, bd_persists = r.bd_persist) b0 = pond(T()) step!("Bd toad", 0, "no treatment", rel(b0), "toads and Bd both go extinct") show_pond(b0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.0, toads_persist = false, bd_persists = false) ``` ::: ::: ### Step 1. A treated class Each year 80% of tadpoles are treated at hatching with a treatment that blocks 90% of infections and lasts the season. ::: {#36 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b1 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9); coverage = 0.8) step!("Bd toad", 1, "treated class: 80% of tadpoles, blocks 90%", rel(b1), "toads saved, Bd eliminated") adults(r) = (r.t[r.t .>= -2], r.A[r.t .>= -2] ./ r.A_disease_free) plot(adults(b0)...; label = "0. no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bd arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", legend = :right) plot!(adults(b1)...; label = "1. tadpoles treated every year") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Unlike Bsal, the simplest treatment works here. The infected stage is short and a new cohort can be treated every year. It does not prevent the initial crash: adults fall to a few percent of their former number before Bd dies out and the population recovers over two decades. ### Step 2. Protection is lost ::: {#38 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b2 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8) step!("Bd toad", 2, "+ protection lost, half-life 18 days", rel(b2), "still works: the season is short") show_pond(b2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.86, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = false) ``` ::: ::: ### Step 3. Stop treating and rely on spread Can treatment stop after five years if the bacteria persist in the pond and reach new tadpoles from there? ::: {#40 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b3 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9, environmental = 50.0, reservoir_half_life = 1.0); coverage = 0.8, treat_years = 0:4) step!("Bd toad", 3, "+ treat 5 years only, bacteria persist in pond", rel(b3), "fails once treatment stops") show_pond(b3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.0, toads_persist = false, bd_persists = false) ``` ::: ::: The field trial behind step 8 found that the applied bacterium spread to untreated frogs within days but then declined everywhere, so this step is not rescued by the evidence either. The remaining steps go back to treating every year. ### Step 4. Survival, not fewer infections As in Part A, treatment now lets infected tadpoles live instead of preventing infection. ::: {#42 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b4 = pond(T(tolerance = 0.7); coverage = 0.8) step!("Bd toad", 4, "+ protection as in trials: survive, still infected", rel(b4), "toads persist at lower numbers; Bd is no longer eliminated") show_pond(b4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.62, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = true) ``` ::: ::: The toads are saved, but Bd now stays in the pond for good, so treatment can never stop. ### Step 5. Lower load ::: {#44 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b5 = pond(load_reducing_treatment(0.7); coverage = 0.8) step!("Bd toad", 5, "+ lower load (70%): less death and less shedding", rel(b5), "little changed: untreated tadpoles and the pond keep Bd going") show_pond(b5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.63, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = true) ``` ::: ::: ### Step 6. Infection after metamorphosis Mitchell's model removes every infected tadpole at metamorphosis. Experiments show that toadlets exposed to Bd are infected, that most die, and that some survive (Smith et al. 2022; counts from the compendium). ::: {#46 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} s = parameter_set(:smith2022) survival = 1 - s.deaths_exposed / s.n_exposed stages = PostMetamorphicInfection(metamorph_survival = survival) @printf("toadlet survival after exposure: %.2f\n", survival) c0 = pond(T(); stages) show_pond(c0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` toadlet survival after exposure: 0.29 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (adults = 0.05, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = true) ``` ::: ::: This changes the untreated outcome: with some infected metamorphs surviving, the toads no longer go extinct, and so neither does Bd. The published "both die out" result depended on every infected animal dying. ::: {#48 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} effs = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99] tols = [0.3, 0.7, 1.0] blocking = [rel(pond(T(efficacy = e); coverage = 0.8, stages)) for e in effs] tolerating = [rel(pond(T(tolerance = τ); coverage = 0.8, stages)) for τ in tols] plot(["0.5", "0.9", "0.99"], blocking; marker = :circle, label = "blocks infection (efficacy)", xlabel = "strength of treatment", ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", ylims = (0, 1), legend = :topleft) plot!(["0.5", "0.9", "0.99"], tolerating; marker = :square, label = "survives infection (tolerance 0.3, 0.7, 1.0)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#50 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b6 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9); coverage = 0.8, stages) step!("Bd toad", 6, "+ infected metamorphs can survive (treatment as in step 1)", rel(b6), "blocking infection no longer eliminates Bd or protects well") b6t = pond(T(tolerance = 0.7); coverage = 0.8, stages) step!("Bd toad", 7, "same, with survival-type protection", rel(b6t), "now the better mechanism: the ranking has reversed") (blocking = show_pond(b6), tolerating = show_pond(b6t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (blocking = (adults = 0.09, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = true), tolerating = (adults = 0.75, toads_persist = true, bd_persists = true)) ``` ::: ::: In step 1, blocking infection eliminated Bd. With the more realistic life cycle it does not, and the treatment that lets animals survive infection now does better. **Which mechanism is best depends on a detail of the host's life cycle, not on the treatment.** ### Step 8. How long the bacteria really last With the measured decay, one dose at hatching wanes during the 95-day tadpole season. More doses in the season restore much of it. ::: {#52 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} waning_t = T(tolerance = 0.7, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0) schedules = [("at hatching only", Float64[]), ("+ day 45", [45.0]), ("+ days 30, 60", [30.0, 60.0]), ("+ days 20, 40, 60, 80", [20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0])] doses = [rel(pond(waning_t; coverage = 0.8, stages, redose_days = d)) for (_, d) in schedules] bar(doses; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(schedules)), yflip = true, legend = false, xlabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#54 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} step!("Bd toad", 8, "+ measured decay, one dose at hatching", doses[1], "protection gone before the season ends") step!("Bd toad", 9, "+ three doses per season", doses[3], "about two-thirds of the benefit restored; five doses do better") doses ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{Float64}: 0.056362921491221865 0.14450370239523072 0.5057080690629617 0.8044351451182551 ``` ::: ::: ### Part B summary ::: {#56 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ladder_plot("Bd toad", "adults in years 25 to 35, fraction of disease-free") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## What each piece of realism did ``` {.julia .cell-code} println("| System | Step | Added | Outcome | What changed |") println("|---|---|---|---|---|") for r in ladder @printf("| %s | %d | %s | %.2f | %s |\n", r.system, r.n, r.added, r.outcome, r.note) end ``` | System | Step | Added | Outcome | What changed | |---|---|---|---|---| | Bsal | 0 | no treatment | 0.00 | population collapses within a year | | Bsal | 1 | treated class: blocks 99% of infection, for life | 0.34 | treated adults are safe; their offspring are not | | Bsal | 2 | + protection lost, half-life 1 year | 0.13 | collapse is only delayed | | Bsal | 3 | + microbiome spreads between animals | 1.00 | full protection: the microbiome maintains itself | | Bsal | 4 | + protection as in trials: survive, still infected | 0.02 | fails, and raises transmission: survivors shed for longer | | Bsal | 5 | + lower load (99%): less death and less shedding | 0.18 | partial; survivors remain infected | | Bsal | 6 | + larval stage (treatment as in step 1) | 0.33 | as step 1: recruits still unprotected | | Bsal | 7 | + treat both stages, kept through metamorphosis | 1.00 | full protection with no spread at all | | Bsal | 8 | + measured decay (half-life 5 days), dosed quarterly | 0.06 | fails: protection lasts about a month; monthly dosing reaches 0.28 | | Bd toad | 0 | no treatment | 0.00 | toads and Bd both go extinct | | Bd toad | 1 | treated class: 80% of tadpoles, blocks 90% | 0.98 | toads saved, Bd eliminated | | Bd toad | 2 | + protection lost, half-life 18 days | 0.86 | still works: the season is short | | Bd toad | 3 | + treat 5 years only, bacteria persist in pond | 0.00 | fails once treatment stops | | Bd toad | 4 | + protection as in trials: survive, still infected | 0.62 | toads persist at lower numbers; Bd is no longer eliminated | | Bd toad | 5 | + lower load (70%): less death and less shedding | 0.63 | little changed: untreated tadpoles and the pond keep Bd going | | Bd toad | 6 | + infected metamorphs can survive (treatment as in step 1) | 0.09 | blocking infection no longer eliminates Bd or protects well | | Bd toad | 7 | same, with survival-type protection | 0.75 | now the better mechanism: the ranking has reversed | | Bd toad | 8 | + measured decay, one dose at hatching | 0.06 | protection gone before the season ends | | Bd toad | 9 | + three doses per season | 0.51 | about two-thirds of the benefit restored; five doses do better | Reading down the table: 1. **The answer changed at almost every step**, and it changed direction more than once. A model stopped at step 3 says a self-spreading microbiome is essential for Bsal. Stopped at step 7 it says spread is unnecessary. Stopped at step 8 it says neither is achievable with bacteria that last a few weeks. 2. **How protection works matters more than how strong it is.** Blocking infection and surviving infection give opposite population-level results for Bsal, and swap rank in toads when the life cycle is made more realistic. 3. **Life-cycle detail in the host model changed the conclusions as much as anything in the treatment model.** Larvae in the Bsal model, and surviving metamorphs in the toad model, each overturned a result. 4. **The two systems differ for a structural reason.** A toad cohort passes through a short infected stage once a year and can be re-treated. A salamander must be protected for life against a pathogen that kills in a week. ## What is not in the model - Bacterial abundance is a clock since the last dose, not a state of each animal. Animals that pick up bacteria from others share the clock of the treated ones. - The fold-drop in abundance at which protection is lost has not been measured. - Whether applied bacteria survive metamorphosis has not been measured. - The Bsal model has no recovery from infection and no years between metamorphosis and maturity. The toad model has thresholds standing in for extinction, and adult toads that carry Bd are not yet combined with treatment. - Everything is deterministic. ## References - Harris RN et al.
